title: Beyond Training Time, Test-Time Coordination is Essential for Cooperative MARL
claim: Cooperative teams need an intermittent test-time coordination channel, which splits into two design problems: encoding behaviors and selecting signals.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, bold headings, shared robot icons across panels
description: Three panels read left to right, each with a bold monospace heading. The left panel, 'Problem setup', shows a warehouse icon and robots (Env) linked in a loop with decentralized agents π1..πN (orange box, obs/act every time step) and a coordinator π_C (light-blue box). Team-level state flows to the coordinator, and a dashed coord signal flows back down to the agents. The center panel, 'Design problem I', shows a grey sphere labeled 'How to encode?' with colored dots. Robot icons doing different tasks surround it, such as pushing a box, lifting a pallet, and carrying a box. The caption reads 'representation space Z'. The right panel, 'Design problem II', shows a small sphere with an orange density. It sits next to the cyan question 'When and what to coordinate?', with a robot trajectory curving upward. A blue dashed path realigns with a grey dashed path, and the label reads 'reassign z for trajectory alignment'. Orange marks the agents, cyan marks the coordinator.
caption: Overview of CTME. (Left) Problem setup. At test time, decentralized agents act at every time step from local observations, while a coordinator intermittently maps team-level state $s$ to high-level signals $z$. (Center) Design problem I. The agent learns a behavioral foundation, a space $\mathcal{Z}$ of distinguishable behaviors such as skills, goals, or etc. (Right) Design problem II. The coordinator selects coupled signals $\pi_C(z\mid s)$ in this space. Namely, $z$ is reassigned for trajectory alignment. {All fleet vehicle icons are generated by ChatGPT-6 Astra through multiple prompts.}
abstract: We argue that cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) should treat test-time coordination as part of the problem definition rather than a deployment artifact. Our focus is on long-horizon, centrally monitored cooperative systems such as warehouse robotics, automated storage-and-retrieval systems, and cloud-resource scheduling, where teams share a reward, operate under shifting objectives, and already run with global telemetry at deployment. The dominant paradigm in this regime, centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), uses global information only during training and provides no coordination channel at execution. This is sufficient when agents are weakly coupled or the environment is stationary, but it fails when the team must realign after conditions change. The limitation is structural rather than algorithmic, and more training cannot add a channel that does not exist at execution time. We call this the recoverability gap. To address it, we name the underexplored design space of intermittent test-time coordination as centralized training with mixed execution (CTME), in which a coordinator observes global state and emits high-level signals while agents act locally. CTME is not a particular learning algorithm, but a cooperative MARL problem setting that makes test-time information structure explicit. It specifies team-level information, high-level signals, and update frequency after training, with CTDE recovered as a limit case. We do not argue that CTDE is obsolete. We argue that removing the test-time channel is a modeling choice, not a necessity, and the wrong default when global telemetry is available and teams must recover from drift.
